t:
(a) 
In consultation with the employees of the Federal Aviation Administration and such non-governmental experts in personnel management systems as he may employ, and notwithstanding the provisions of title 5, United States Code, and other Federal personnel laws, the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration shall develop and implement, not later than January 1, 1996, a personnel management system for the Federal Aviation Administration that addresses the unique demands on the agency’s workforce. Such a new system shall, at a minimum, provide for greater flexibility in the hiring, training, compensation, and location of personnel.
 
    (b) 
The provisions of title 5, United States Code, shall not apply to the new personnel management system developed and implemented pursuant to subsection (a), with the exception of—

        (1) 
section 2302(b), relating to whistleblower protection;
 
        (2) 
sections 3308–3320, relating to veterans’ preference;
 
        (3) 
section 7116(b)(7), relating to limitations on the right to strike;
 
        (4) 
section 7204, relating to antidiscrimination;
 
        (5) 
chapter 73, relating to suitability, security, and conduct;
 
        (6) 
chapter 81, relating to compensation for work injury; and
 
        (7) 
chapters 83–85, 87, and 89, relating to retirement, unemployment compensation, and insurance coverage.
  
    (c) 
This section shall take effect on April 1, 1996.

fable.w: The Administrator must develop and implement a new personnel management system, a federal decision rather than a mere study, in consultation with non-governmental experts, who are by the statute's own terms outside the federal government. The tempting "No" reading is that the consultation is only with FAA employees (intra-government) or that the experts become federal because the Administrator "may employ" them. That reading is weaker because the text expressly calls them non-governmental and ties their input to the design of the system.
fable.s: In consultation with the employees of the Federal Aviation Administration and such non-governmental experts in personnel management systems as he may employ

opus.w: The Administrator must develop and implement a new personnel management system (a federal decision) in consultation with 'non-governmental experts in personnel management systems,' who are outside the federal government. Consulting FAA employees alone would be intra-government and would not count. But the statute explicitly calls the experts non-governmental, so the consultation crosses the federal boundary. It is also tied to an actual policy decision, not just the contents of a study.
opus.s: In consultation with the employees of the Federal Aviation Administration and such non-governmental experts in personnel management systems as he may employ, and notwithstanding the provisions of title 5, United States Code, and other Federal personnel laws, the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration shall develop and implement
opus.b:
1. **Thinking it through.** The tempting reading is "No." On that reading, the consultation stays inside the government: FAA employees are federal employees, and experts "he may employ" would become federal staff. That reading doesn't hold up. The statute expressly calls the experts "non-governmental," which points to outside consultants rather than agency staff. The Administrator must consult them before making a real federal decision: designing and putting in place a new FAA personnel management system. That is consultation with outsiders before a federal decision, not a study or a report to Congress. My remaining doubt is whether "employ" turns these experts into federal insiders.

2. **Label.**

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Administrator to develop a personnel system in consultation with FAA employees and experts he employs. FAA employees are inside the federal government. The experts are employed by the agency to assist in the development, functioning as part of the internal process rather than as independent outside stakeholders participating in a decision (such as through an advisory board or public comment). This constitutes internal agency management and coordination, not participation by outside parties.
qwen_chat.s: In consultation with the employees of the Federal Aviation Administration and such non-governmental experts in personnel management systems as he may employ... the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration shall develop and implement... a personnel management system
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "non-governmental experts" are outside parties, so their involvement constitutes participation. However, the text says the Administrator may "employ" them. If they are employed by the federal agency to perform a task, they are acting as federal employees or contractors for the purpose of that work, not as independent outside stakeholders participating in a decision-making process (like an advisory board or public comment). Furthermore, the primary consultation is with "employees of the Federal Aviation Administration," who are inside the government. The definition explicitly excludes intra-government coordination and applications/employment. The key is whether the outside party is consulted *before* a decision in a participatory capacity (like an advisory role or public hearing) or is simply hired to do the work. Here, they are employed to help develop the system. More importantly, the definition states: "If every actor involved in participation is inside the federal government, the answer is 'No'". The FAA employees are inside. The experts are employed by the FAA. This is internal agency development.

Wait, let's re-read carefully. "In consultation with... such non-governmental experts... as he may employ". If they are employed, they are effectively part of the agency's workforce for this project. The definition says "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government...". It lists "experts" as outside people. But it also says "federal employees are all INSIDE". If the experts are *employed* by the FAA, are they federal employees? Likely contractors or temporary hires. But the crucial distinction in the "No" traps is "consultation or coordination BETWEEN federal agencies or federal officials". This is the Administrator consulting with his own employees and hired experts. This is internal management. It is not a public hearing, advisory board with independent members, or consultation with states/tribes/public. It is the agency head developing a policy with his staff and hired help. This is internal decision-making.

Therefore, the label is No.
